To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

consciousness is a function of the brain, that it is a function of three types of internal representation, that the first two of these types are supported by the empirical data, and that the third is a plausible extrapolation from the first two.

the three categories of internal representation are the following: (1) the representations that are the content of phenomenal experience (the qualia), which are the states of the brain that have the property of phenomenal consciousness; (2) the representations that have the property called access consciousness, which are the contents of consciousness in the common sense of the word; and (3) the representations that support the conscious will, which are the states that have the property that is the basis for the feeling of volition.

consciousness is the result of a process in which three categories of representations interact in the brain: (1) representations that are associated with a particular modality of perception, such as vision, audition, or touch; (2) representations of the self and of one’s own mental states and processes; and (3) representations that are not tied to any modality, and are therefore more general in character.

The main takeaway from our work is that

consciousness is a property of the brain that can be defined as the ability of the organism to have a representation of its internal state, a definition that is both physically and functionally precise, and that it can be studied in the neuroscience laboratories of today.
consciousness is a biological property of the organism that is not reducible to any of its component parts.
